sections.title: 01 / What this season teaches
sections.text:
## More capability arrived; reliability and coordination remained the constraint

The strongest opportunity is to make the existing drivetrain, intake, hopper and shooter cooperate reliably. Fixing autonomous stages that cannot finish, continuously managing shot readiness, and protecting electrical headroom are more defensible priorities than increasing top speed.

**Three distinct stories matter.** Front-right drive feedback was already missing in March 12 practice and remained absent during Tabernacle Q7 and Q11. In Q11, a separate brief roboRIO input-voltage collapse preceded a long output/communications interruption. By Q53, front-right feedback was responsive again. Bensalem then showed richer robot behavior, stronger alliance results, and recurring low-voltage and shooting-readiness concerns.

This retrospective covers the **supplied January–March 29 archive**, with later Git development through May discussed separately. It is not evidence of every event or every robot configuration in 2026. Of 136 supplied log files, nine are empty. The broader swerve scan retains four decode-error prefixes; the earlier narrower triage reported three. Successful decoding does not establish that a file contains a complete match. There are 29 recorded match appearances at two events, but enabled gameplay telemetry for only **11 qualifications and two playoffs**.

**Evidence labels:** observations are logged values or explicitly reviewed video frames; code findings describe a retained revision; hypotheses describe possible causes; recommendations are proposed experiments. A code commit is not proof of deployment, and a match win is not an individual-robot score.

sections.title: 02 / Competition results
sections.text:
## The competitive picture improved, with an uneven finish

At the March 14–15 event in Tabernacle, named the **FMA District Seneca Event** in the broadcast, 1257's qualification alliance record was **3–9**. At Bensalem on March 28–29 it was **7–4–1**. Playoff records were 1–2 and 0–2 respectively. Across these 29 appearances, the alliance record was **11–17–1**.

Qualification alliance scores averaged **87.5 at Tabernacle** and **141.8 at Bensalem**; medians were **65.5** and **138.5**. These are descriptive alliance outcomes, including partners and penalties. They do not isolate robot contribution, schedule difficulty, defense, or shooting accuracy.

Bensalem Q2's **258–44** was the highest qualification alliance score in the retained results, but no enabled robot log is supplied. Q34's **148–73** is a more useful technical baseline because it contains a full teleop interval with sustained mechanism activity. Tabernacle Q63's **145–140** is an interesting close win, but the log ends early, so its finish cannot be reconstructed from robot telemetry.

The late Bensalem sequence—Q42 **63–88**, Q48 **29–242**, Q53 **47–221**, then Q61 **123–70**—shows why we should inspect individual failure modes rather than tell a simple continuous-improvement story. Q42's data quality and device-health warnings make it unsuitable as a healthy low-current comparison.

The complete match ledger below links to each result. “No enabled gameplay data” means an evidence gap, not that the robot was inactive.

sections.title: 03 / Build season → first event
sections.text:
## From inherited platform to coordinated shooter



### January: inherited drive platform

Jan 13 [e14861b](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/e14861bb461ef8786fa4503f270b22e75c5cf92d) imports the previous platform; Jan 21 [4e7c726](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/4e7c7261efc0f98eeaaea50897b97bb0b7b7e0d5) updates CAN IDs.

January tests have changing four-module feedback. January 28 has an encoder-only front-right anomaly, followed by recovery that day.

Basic driving was available early. That encoder-only episode differs from March's absent electrical and encoder feedback.


### February: mechanisms and test infrastructure

Hood/flywheel/kicker/hopper implementations, simulations, late-February rewrites and tuning utilities ([45b3940](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/45b3940fd094e096b0e3f51723ad67b433935040) adds tunable numbers).

February 25 has an extended practice run with responsive front-right feedback; the archive also has many disabled/short tests.

The software grew from separate mechanism bring-up toward shared control. Commit titles do not certify mechanisms physically worked.


### March 7–13: geometry, shooting and autonomous integration

[ad5d9ba](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/ad5d9ba044520c334cb12be72b20429d13e9d245) changes three steering offsets and changes encoder offset addition to subtraction. March 8–12 adds/adjusts hub aiming, shooting tables and autos; [1760063](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/17600639e7565efb617f53e4880615b5eaa283f6) is the March 12 logged base, [f0e5fc8](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/f0e5fc88cf38aa3a792dafdaf0b42a1e975c38d6) the first-event base.

March 12 practice already has persistent front-right drive feedback loss. Tabernacle Q7/Q11 retain it.

The March 7 swerve fix concerns steering coordinate calibration; it did not prevent the later drive-controller telemetry anomaly. These should not be called the same bug.


### March 15: first-event adjustments

[f085965](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/f0859657e95d44ee51d464435b274831b56b6c5e) and [83e550c](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/83e550cf1e2da4d1364696ba21d60533cc01905b), merged in [4e45023](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/4e45023884010585488d5b7f0716f24c4f2afb4b), modify controls, paths and shooting calibration. Lookup-table distance keys shift outward by 0.3429 m, changing which speed/hood value is requested for a pose. A 1.5 s teleop readiness timeout is introduced in the merged code.

Q53 has responsive front-right speed/position/current/voltage; Q58/Q63 also do.

Feedback availability recovered, but the committed drive files are unchanged between Q11/Q53. No repair record or exact dirty source explains the recovery. The table shift is a calibration change, not proof earlier shots were short/long.


### March 16–23: reliability, load and mechanism changes

[fd60dd9](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/fd60dd9f29a56d4eb8cbbca00038811ced1e9285) reduces six mechanism current limits to 40 A. Later commits revise limits again. [7ea645a](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/7ea645a532e904f733fff73aa9adaec915aa38f4) removes climb software and adds energy logging; [01c9126](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/01c91268c1e2d0c4a3267fdc1a94402a846ae674) adds subsystem connection alerts/telemetry; [975d4a7](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/975d4a77c3083c7f6096a2ac6bf20129d5f23ee5) adds a second hopper-intake motor in software. Hood/pivot/voltage clamps are added.

Later logs expose more device telemetry, making earlier/later availability comparisons uneven.

These are concrete attempts to address robustness and mechanism operation. Removing climb code does not establish mechanical removal or failure. Two-motor support suggests hardware/configuration evolution but is not a physical inspection.


### March 18–23: vision experiments

Limelight-related work appears, followed by [a10f56f](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/a10f56faf81e014419b15c3629da0db23e614956) returning toward PhotonVision; [aa2546d](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/aa2546d487affa6056514b2f25859d612b20bdee) changes drive/vision integration.

Camera connectivity and estimator corrections are visible, but complete accepted/rejected observation histories were not logged.

Vision architecture was being iterated. Connection flags are insufficient to rank pose accuracy or conclude a camera was physically broken.


### March 21–29: faster feeding and richer driver/auto behavior

[3189eff](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/3189eff2507e8035d78510e5b1cf7ee75dc158d9) removes the 1.5 s timeout; [01c9126](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/01c91268c1e2d0c4a3267fdc1a94402a846ae674) reinstates a shorter 0.5 s timeout. [9004231](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/90042317e3d8f740d00aa73eb4fdcd3a5d4ecfa1)/[6b19b9d](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/6b19b9d3a1d8d6b29cd83ea54ead8449c51efd7c) revise point-and-lock behavior. [4517e0c](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/4517e0c20f07dfecdc2b3d688a83379b86066aa2) adds paths and sweep/outpost options; [90560c0](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/90560c085c003ecd8c9b095de77cf99add8ea402) adds idle spin during a return path. [5083ee8](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/5083ee80a875e8ab8ca3d9f7e376bda174516c6f) adds both trench headings. [eaa6f81](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/eaa6f817b1270b3cac850423deb50fbcf3b93e2f) waits for hub alignment before selecting lock/drive and adds an alignment predicate to feeding.

Bensalem has responsive front-right feedback in usable runs, but repeated low-voltage operation and feeding with readiness false. Q34 has no kicker output during autonomous; Q48 later records autonomous kicker output on the same sweep selection.

More capability did not eliminate coordination/tuning constraints. Q34 versus Q48 is suggestive of readiness/timing variability, not a clean before/after experiment.


### After the supplied competition logs

March 31 [192680a](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/192680aa39633b7dcee2b1fcfce88272c4e502fd) introduces Paralib work; April adds tunable persistence/periodic changes; May 26 [4b7ed85](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/4b7ed8589f9479cedd70fc11c49ba38d68c4c9be) refactors vision toward Limelight/PhotonVision IO on a later branch.

No supplied match telemetry validates those later changes.

Describe them as subsequent development, not demonstrated season recovery or scoring improvement.

figures.caption: Actual GitHub diff, March 7, commit [ad5d9ba](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/commit/ad5d9ba044520c334cb12be72b20429d13e9d245). Three steering offsets change and encoder-offset addition becomes subtraction. This calibrates steering coordinates; it does not explain the later loss of drive voltage/current feedback.

sections.title: 04 / The front-right issue
sections.text:
## It started before Q11—and it recovered by Q53

January 28 has an earlier, different anomaly: front-right speed and position remain zero while reported current reaches **66.81 A** and voltage changes. Later runs that day recover. That pattern points first toward feedback/encoder validity, whereas the March episode also lacks drive electrical feedback.

The last brief responsive pre-event run is February 26; February 25 provides the stronger long comparison. On **March 12**, the 22:37 practice prefix and 23:09 recording already show front-right drive position, speed and voltage at zero, with current at most about **0.110 A**, while steering changes and other modules move. The exact onset lies in the gap between supplied tests.

Tabernacle Q7 contains **76.601 seconds** of qualifying peer motion with front-right speed at zero. Q11 contains **35.159 seconds** under that comparison condition, and its six retained drive feedback fields remain at their initial zero values throughout. At about FPGA **416 s**, optimized front-right speed is **4.591 m/s** while measured speed is zero; other modules report approximately 2.2–2.7 m/s.

By Q53 the feedback is responsive: at **180.235015 s**, front-right command is −4.600 m/s, measured speed −3.143 m/s, applied voltage −9.194 V and current 19.963 A. Across 32.641 s of qualifying peer motion, only 0.040 s has near-zero front-right speed, with no sustained ≥0.5 s interval. Q58 and Q63 also show recovery in their retained windows.

**What changed physically is unknown.** The three committed drive files are identical between the Q11 and Q53 bases. Both deployments have uncommitted changes; there is no repair record. Power, CAN, controller configuration and read validity are candidates. Measured speed and odometry share encoder inputs, so they are not independent proof of wheel motion. The recorded base maps Module 1 to front-right drive CAN ID 12 and steer ID 11; verify the actual machine before tracing wiring.

figures.caption: Native AdvantageScope at approximately 416 s in Q11. Orange optimized states versus blue measured states reveal the front-right command/feedback mismatch before the power event.
Derived comparison from original log timestamps: Q11 versus Tabernacle Q53. The later log is a responsive-feedback comparison, not a complete-match repair certificate.

sections.title: 05 / Q11: the electrical case study
sections.text:
## A short power disturbance, then a long loss of control



### Before 417

Module 1 drive current, applied voltage, velocity and position remain zero for the entire recording. At 415.993482 its optimized speed command is 4.591 m/s; its measured speed is 0. Other modules have nonzero feedback.

An established command/feedback mismatch before the brownout. The recorded base code labels Module 1 as front-right, CAN drive ID 12. The dirty deployed working tree prevents treating that base mapping as fully verified. An unpowered/unreachable/misconfigured controller or an input/logging problem are candidates; zero feedback does not prove physical motor failure.


### 417.513339–417.553555

First BrownedOut=true pulse; SystemActive and 6 V Active go false and recover.

First recorded protection event in this incident. It is not proof that the processor rebooted.


### 417.593364–417.633691

Second pulse; controller input reports 4.0357585 V, below logged 6.75 V threshold. It reports 12.3663 V at 417.613342. 5 V and 3.3 V active flags remain true.

Very short controller-input disturbance and recovery, with selective rail/output protection.


### 417.613342–417.633691

Raw PDH fault mask changes 1048624→34603056→1048624; delta is bit 25, named CAN-warning by the declared logger's packing scheme.

A coincident raw diagnostic change requiring logger verification. It does not locate a wire or establish a breaker trip.


### 417.733435

CommsDisableCount 0→1; SystemActive stays false until 475.138153.

A 57.405 s output-disable interval begins. Power voltage recovery does not mean robot control recovered.


### 418.082935

All three camera-connected flags become false.

Vision communication is unavailable. This does not mean three camera power circuits failed independently.


### 419.436974

Radio-status connected flag becomes false; status payload unavailable.

Radio reachability check fails. Status polling and timeout delays mean this is not necessarily when the radio physically lost power/link.


### 422.605110

DSAttached, FMSAttached and Enabled become false.

Driver Station/field attachment flags catch up later. These delays cannot establish a precise physical failure cascade.


### 473.995065

Radio becomes reachable. Reported 6 GHz rxBytes drop from 8,760,055 at 413.932707 to 336; txBytes drop from 279,590,768 to 861.

Consistent with a radio restart or interface/counter reset. There is no radio uptime/boot-counter measurement here to distinguish those possibilities.


The roboRIO continues producing cycle timestamps through this interval. The largest cycle-timestamp gap between 410 and 480 s is 0.128848 s, not 57 s; the largest logged FullCycleMS during 417–418 s is 23.299 ms. A sustained roboRIO processor reboot or minute-long robot-code freeze is therefore poorly supported. This does not rule out a short disturbance or watchdog/communication effects.

### What the currents tell us

The robot had substantial earlier load: PDH total current is 128 A at the held sample for 415 s and 138 A near 416 s. Individual motor-controller current readings also show activity. These motor readings are controller-reported output currents, not interchangeable with PDH battery-side channel currents; do not sum or equate them to identify wiring.

Immediately around the controller minimum, PDH voltage samples bracket it at 12.328125 V at 417.573348 and 12.3515625 V at 417.633691, with total currents 2 A and 4 A. The PDH updates much more slowly than the controller protection flags. These samples argue against a **sustained** whole-robot high-current sag at the exact failure, but cannot exclude a short main-power transient between samples. They do not prove the disturbance was confined to the roboRIO branch.

### PDH data-quality correction

Q11 identifies base commit `f0e5fc88cf38aa3a792dafdaf0b42a1e975c38d6` and marks its working tree **uncommitted**. That commit declares AdvantageKit 26.0.0. The upstream 26.0.0 native PDH reader source contains suspicious channel indexing and fault-packing operations: channel 3 is overwritten by reads intended for 4/5; channels 18–23 reference status 2 data in the status 3 block; multiple fault-mask updates use the existing mask in the combination where newly decoded bits would ordinarily be expected.

**Applicability to the deployed binary is unproven.** The recorded arrays do not consistently match every simple prediction of those source defects. A patched/rebuilt binary or another source/binary difference remains possible. We therefore preserve all 24 recorded current values, highlight channels 3–5 and 18–23 amber for decoder review, and show raw PDH fault masks as warnings rather than certified physical faults. Do not conclude that channels 4, 5 or 20 tripped merely because their bits appear in the baseline raw mask; 1048624 was already present at 13.949315 s, long before this incident.

Before using those channels for wiring diagnosis, verify the actual deployed native library and compare against an independent, trusted PDH current/fault reading. Do not fabricate corrected historical channel currents by copying or shifting other channels.

Source: [AdvantageKit 26.0.0 PDH reader](https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit/blob/v26.0.0/akit/src/main/native/cc/pdp_reader.cc), saved under the retained local provenance archive. [Recorded base dependency file](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot/blob/f0e5fc88cf38aa3a792dafdaf0b42a1e975c38d6/vendordeps/AdvantageKit.json). Both are source observations, not a verified deployed-binary inspection.

### Ranked potential causes

These are engineering hypotheses, not measured probabilities.

1. **Intermittent control-electronics power or ground connection.** The brief 4.04 V controller reading, continuing roboRIO logging and later network reset symptoms make a control-power feed, terminal, crimp, ground return or associated power hardware a strong investigation target. If radio and RIO feeds are independent, a fault only in the RIO positive lead would not explain a real radio restart by itself; inspect their shared upstream power/ground and the radio supply path too.
2. **A short interruption in the main battery/connector/breaker path.** A connector, cable termination or breaker connection can briefly interrupt power during robot motion. The slower PDH sampling could miss the lowest voltage, and earlier high loads provide context. A weak battery or excessive main-path resistance is possible, but the low nearby logged current means a sustained motor-load sag alone is not established.
3. **Radio supply/PoE/regulator or network-interface reset.** Loss of all camera connections and the radio traffic-counter reset support investigating the radio and its power/network path. A radio-only issue does not explain the controller 4.04 V observation; a shared power disturbance or a second issue would still be needed.
4. **A primary CAN-only fault or software stall.** Lower on current evidence. The PDH's raw CAN-warning bit merits examination, but the selected roboRIO CAN counters do not establish a leading bus failure, and a CAN-only explanation does not account well for controller undervoltage plus radio counter resets. The onset loop timing does not show a long robot-code stall.

Do not connect the preexisting Module 1 anomaly causally to the brownout without further evidence. It could reduce available drive performance or reflect missing telemetry, but it does not by itself explain a controller power dip.

### Next discriminating checks

With robot power off, have the electrical subteam inspect and verify the battery/main-breaker connections, RIO power terminals, shared ground returns, radio supply and Ethernet/PoE connections. Compare RIO and PDH input voltage with independently trustworthy instrumentation during a controlled, supervised load/movement test. Confirm the actual PDH channel map and installed logger binary before interpreting channel faults. Check the Module 1 drive controller's expected CAN ID, power, CAN reachability and vendor diagnostics; log per-device communication/error flags and bus voltage instead of relying on zero current as a connectivity test.

figures.caption: Native AdvantageScope at FPGA 417.593364 s: the RIO/battery-input and 6 V indicators are red. The logical connections are a teaching schematic, not a verified wiring diagram. Amber PDH channels require decoder review; they do not prove overcurrent or tripped breakers.

sections.title: 06 / Put the broadcast beside the signals
sections.text:
## The video establishes context, not the failed connector

[Watch the official FIRST Mid-Atlantic Q11 recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=durFirbjol0). The alignment is **raw log seconds = video seconds + 384.057**, with about **±1 second uncertainty**. At video 33.5 s, the broadcast shows **2:12 remaining**, red 23 and blue 45. This is the visual neighborhood of the 417.5–417.6 s brownout pulses. The synchronization cannot resolve their millisecond ordering.

The initial roboRIO protection pulses occur before the radio and Driver Station timeout flags. At FPGA 417.733 s, SystemActive becomes false; the radio status flag falls around 419.437 s, and DS/FMS attachment and Enabled fall around 422.605 s. **Polling delays prevent interpreting that sequence as the exact physical order in which devices lost power.**

Radio reachability returns around 473.995 s. DS attachment and enable return at 475.138 s, corresponding to video about 91.1 s. The disabled/DS-detached interval is **52.533 s**; the earlier SystemActive-low interval is **57.405 s**. These measure different states and should not be mixed. Intake and kicker activity resume afterward, while low input voltage remains an issue.

The reviewed video evidence consists of paused frames across Q11, Q34 and Q42, plus focused native replay checks—not continuously counted full matches. Several bumpers are small or occluded. No collision, individual shot count, missed-fuel count or physical wiring failure is assigned from these frames. The advancing alliance score during 1257's interruption includes other robots.

For an electronics-subteam walkthrough, first follow the command/feedback mismatch, then the voltage notch, then SystemActive and CommsDisableCount, and only then radio/DS recovery. Ask why Enabled can remain stored true while outputs are unavailable, and why a slower 12.3 V PDH sample cannot disprove a brief RIO dip.

figures.caption: Official FIRST Mid-Atlantic broadcast, Q11, video 33.5 s. The visible clock is 2:12; this is approximately FPGA 417.557 s. Source: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=durFirbjol0&t=33s). Still reproduced for technical commentary; no full broadcast is hosted here.

Same official broadcast at video 96 s, after the logged attachment recovery. Overlay reads red 78, blue 150. This is a live score, not the final 123–193 result. [Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=durFirbjol0&t=96s).

sections.title: 07 / Bensalem: progress and remaining limits
sections.text:
## Q34 is the useful working baseline; Q48 exposes the load problem

**Q34:** in 140.014 s of teleop, intake is active for 88.349 s, kicker for 42.004 s, and flywheel above 100 rad/s for 63.115 s. Flywheel connectivity stays true. That is meaningful operating time, although it does not measure scored fuel. During autonomous there is no kicker activity despite flywheel activity. Near its end, measured speed is 324.276 rad/s against 328.938 rad/s requested; the hood is ready, but flywheel readiness is false under the retained ±2.5 rad/s tolerance.

**Q48:** the robot logs 119.694 s of drive-voltage activity but only 14.220 s of kicker activity. Voltage spends **67.837 of 140.046 teleop seconds below 9 V**, compared with Q34's **34.622 of 140.014 s**. Its minimum is 6.982 V. This is a strong reason to investigate combined demand and route efficiency, but traffic, defense, ball supply, battery condition and wiring resistance are unresolved confounders.

**Q53 and Q61:** below-9-V teleop durations are 59.392/140.080 s and 57.229/140.008 s. Q61 wins at alliance level despite substantial low-voltage time. A win does not certify a healthy electrical system. Nine volts is an exploratory diagnostic threshold, not the roboRIO brownout threshold.

**Feeding versus readiness:** Q34 has 29.040 s of kicker activity with flywheel readiness false; Q48 has 12.275 s and Q53 has 22.126 s. Feeding can itself pull speed down, the tolerance may be too tight, an override may be active, or one-time readiness gating may permit continued feeding. These overlaps do not count missed shots.

**Q42:** all four drive modules are near zero, multiple fields are implausible, flywheel connectivity is false and recorded intake/kicker activity is zero. It carries a broad device/telemetry-health warning, not a proven isolated front-right failure. A high unloaded voltage is not a useful healthy comparison. Q34 and Q42 share a Git base but both are dirty builds, so even that comparison does not establish identical executable code.

sections.title: 08 / Read the robot as a system
sections.text:
## What the electrical and mechanism views can tell you

The AdvantageScope workspace includes **24 raw PDH channel-current traces**, an electrical logical map, drive/steer/mechanism motor details, CAN diagnostics, rail and connection states, driver inputs, alerts, measured-versus-commanded swerve states, and schematic Mechanism2d views. All panels share a time cursor so a warning can be compared with commands and sensor response.

Use the PDH channels by number until the actual wiring map is documented. There is no defensible channel-to-motor assignment from these logs alone. Controller-reported motor currents are not interchangeable with battery-side PDH current; PWM operation and reporting semantics differ. Current bars have a display scale, while the underlying values remain available. Gray means missing/unknown; amber can mean uncertain decoding or a command/feedback mismatch; it does not always mean a failed component.

Mechanism2d shows measured encoder angles against goals for the hood and hopper. Arm lengths and placements are schematic, and encoder zero is not certified horizontal. Swerve measured-versus-setpoint views expose tracking disagreement, but a shared sensor failure can also corrupt odometry. The 3D robot is an approximate visualization rather than fabrication CAD.

Camera viewpoints use code-derived transforms. The field pose is an estimator output, not ground truth, and a pose jump may be a reset or vision correction. Connection flags do not prove good vision. Complete per-observation tag IDs, freshness, ambiguity and acceptance/rejection reasons were not present historically; new telemetry can support future analysis but cannot retroactively create missing observations.

For a repeatable review: open a match, choose a known timestamp, compare the electrical map with its exact value table, switch to swerve and mechanisms without moving the cursor, then check timing and video. Native AdvantageScope's video source/offset is not fully restored by a saved layout; select the paired file and lock it. The local synchronized browser player retains the reviewed per-match alignments.

figures.caption: Native AdvantageScope motor map at approximately 416 s. Reported motor current/voltage and connection evidence help prioritize investigation; schematic grouping does not establish the physical PDH wiring.
Native AdvantageScope Mechanism2d at approximately 416 s. Measured encoder angles and goals are visible together; geometry is illustrative.

sections.title: 09 / The software I would change first
sections.text:
## Retain the hardware; improve the coordination layer


### 1. Give autonomous stages explicit completion and failure behavior

This is the clearest static correctness opportunity. In the Bensalem base:

- RIGHT_TRENCH chains `followPathFileCommand("RNZ_RS").alongWith(flywheel.runIdle())` before scoring. `runIdle()` is a continuous command, so the parallel group does not normally finish when the path finishes. Use a path deadline so the spin-up command ends with the path and scoring can start.
- DEPOT places continuous `hopperPivot.runIntakeAngle()` between the first scoring timeout and `DEPOT_END`. Without an end condition, the later path is unreachable in that source. Make positioning a finite, bounded stage and hold the mechanism through an appropriate parallel/default control afterward.
- An initial `.until(atGoal())` can wait indefinitely when feedback never reaches the predicate. Give positioning/alignment bounded success/failure outcomes; on failure choose a conservative fallback rather than silently advancing as though successful.

These conclusions follow WPILib's composition semantics: `alongWith` waits for all members, whereas a deadline ends its companions when the deadline command ends. [Official WPILib documentation](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/command-compositions.html).

Do not claim these exact bugs caused a particular match's failed auto. Some RIGHT_TRENCH logs record autonomous feeding despite the committed base's blocking construction, which is further reason to inspect the actual dirty deployment. No command-stage transition trace exists to resolve the discrepancy.

Verification: run every chooser option in scheduler simulation, assert that intended stage transitions occur, inject missing position feedback and path failure, and assert the fallback. Log selected auto and every stage's enter/exit/reason. This has a clearer acceptance condition than judging an auto by its name or an alliance score.

### 2. Replace the shooting expression with a continuously evaluated shot coordinator

This is my highest expected scoring-throughput improvement, provided the robot is electrically healthy. The teleop expression `waitUntil(ready).withTimeout(0.5).andThen(feed)` advances after either readiness OR timeout; the timeout is not a successful readiness check. Once feeding starts, readiness is not continuously reapplied by that expression. The earlier Q11 base also waits only once before feeding, even without the timeout.

Use explicit idle, spin-up/aim, ready, feed, recover and fault states. Compute one coherent distance/hood/speed/heading solution per cycle. Require valid device feedback and a stable measured speed/hood/heading before normal feeding; pause or reduce feeding when speed falls below a separately calibrated recovery boundary. Use hysteresis to avoid oscillation. Include target validity/range, pose confidence and suitable chassis speed. Provide a deliberate, logged driver override if desired; a spin-up timeout should report inability to become ready, not silently impersonate success.

Combine this with measured flywheel feedforward/PID tuning and empirical shot-table calibration at repeatable distances. Pre-spin only when a shot is likely and power headroom permits. Existing command architecture has the ingredients; coordinating them is the missing piece. Without a ball sensor or manually labeled video, commanded feeding time is not actual throughput, so validate with counted successful shots and recovery time on the same hardware.

Also fix wrapped heading error in `isHubAligned()`: simple subtraction can report a nearly full-turn error across the ±π boundary. Review the one-time `Commands.either` choice after alignment; it is not a continuously reevaluated transition between locked and driving states. These are source-level corner cases, not measured causes of season losses.

### 3. Manage combined power demand

Prefer bounded acceleration, smooth flywheel ramps and coordinated intake/agitation/feed demand to blanket increases in current limits. Preserve steering/control authority and shot stability when voltage falls; restore limits with hysteresis rather than rapid switching. Tune under representative multi-mechanism load, not only one subsystem at a time. Account for the fact that reduced acceleration or idle spin can trade energy against cycle time; measure it.

Use trusted battery-side current and voltage for the power model. Controller motor currents cannot simply be summed and multiplied by battery voltage to obtain battery power under PWM operation. The existing EnergyLogger does that approximation, assumes 0.5 A for the radio, and uses fixed cycle time. Treat it as an estimate, or replace it with calibrated battery-side measurements and measured elapsed time. The previously identified PDH source-quality concerns must be resolved before using that stream as a closed-loop authority.

### 4. Make device failures impossible to mistake for valid zeros

Extend the March alert work to each swerve drive and steering controller. Log last successful update, individual read/configuration/setpoint errors, bus voltage, reset/fault information, device identity and configuration revision. Alert clearly when commanded motion plus moving peers produces invalid or persistently zero feedback; avoid declaring a failure from a normal stationary wheel.

Before each match, a deliberate supervised preflight should confirm all four drive/steering feedback paths, gyro, shooting devices and camera freshness. Do not automatically spin motors on enable or mask a fault with invented measurements. A driver-visible health summary and a logged override are more useful than blindly allowing full-performance autonomous operation with unknown odometry.

### 5. Make localization and deployment repeatable

The PhotonVision implementation returns cached results when no new unread frames arrive. The drive layer can reconsider these at old timestamps without an explicit per-camera consumed-timestamp gate. Process each observation once, reject stale/out-of-order/implausible estimates, and log observation age, tag IDs, ambiguity, uncertainty and acceptance/rejection reason. Fix bounds validation before indexing vision arrays. Evaluate against replay scenarios and known field measurements; do not infer accuracy from camera connectivity.

Save exact deployed source/configuration, controller IDs, camera transforms, path hashes and shot-table revision with each log. Dirty-build metadata made several otherwise promising comparisons impossible. This is a direct debugging/time-to-repair improvement even when it does not change a control loop.

sections.title: 10 / Driver and autonomous strategy
sections.text:
## Reduce the number of things that must go right at once

**Before queueing:** use a supervised health check that confirms all four drive/steer feedback paths, gyro, shooter and fresh cameras. Record battery identity and failed checks. A stationary 12 V reading is insufficient; compare behavior under a repeatable controlled load. Never automatically spin motors just to run a health test on enable.

**Autonomous:** begin with one repeatable first release and a short collection–return route. Give each stage a bounded completion condition, log its transition, and define a conservative fallback. Optimize distance and acceleration only after every intended stage finishes reliably. Coordinate starting position and lanes with partners; chooser names do not establish that a route completed.

**Driver operation:** test two or three calibrated stationary shooting locations and shorter collect–return–settle–shoot cycles. Prefer a clear ready/recovering cue over making the driver infer flywheel speed. Choose alliance collection lanes in advance. Schedule collection/repositioning around the official hub-activity rules, with an explicit unknown state when game data is missing. Historical inactive-window waste cannot be counted reliably from this archive.

**Measure actual outcomes:** count shots made and attempted, first-valid-shot latency, recovery time between releases, successful shots per opportunity, driver overrides and device uptime. Use full video review and a controlled test sheet, not kicker-on time as a scoring proxy. Compare the same distances, batteries and mechanism settings. The archive supports these experiments but does not support an extra-points forecast.

**Endgame:** establish a shared access plan and a time budget with alliance partners. The removal of climb software is not proof that the physical climber failed or was removed; no measured climb success rate is established here.

sections.title: 11 / A better robot archetype
sections.text:
## My design direction: a dependable collector with a controlled stationary shot

This is a **design hypothesis**, not a claim that the available evidence identifies the globally optimal 2026 robot. Given these logs, I would favor a robot that collects efficiently, buffers fuel reliably, settles quickly, and meters fuel into a well-calibrated shooter. Keep the capable swerve platform, but make four-module health and service access non-negotiable.

The conceptual flow is **wide compliant intake → low-jam buffer → controlled metering → repeatable shooter**. Prioritize a clear, accessible fuel path and robust sensing over adding more independent motions. A fixed or limited-adjustment hood is worth comparing with the present adjustable design if it can cover the required shooting locations; reduced flexibility could buy simpler calibration and faster readiness. That trade must be tested on the field, not assumed.

A turret or shoot-on-the-move system could increase opportunity, but would add localization, aiming, packaging and tuning requirements to a robot already showing coordination and power concerns. I would require reliable stationary scoring first. A climb mechanism should earn its mass, space and development time through measured success and alliance strategy; this archive cannot supply that calculation.

Electronics packaging should make terminals, controller indicators, CAN segments and radio supply accessible and labeled. Preserve strain relief and deliberate cable routing, with documented PDH channel assignments and controller identities. Add instrumentation that distinguishes invalid/stale readings from valid zeros. These are serviceability goals, not a reconstructed wiring diagram.

**Acceptance gates before adding complexity:** repeatable intake without frequent intervention; a measured successful-feed rate across battery states; bounded autonomous completion; trustworthy pose and device health; and sustained combined-load tests without unexplained control interruptions. Select the simplest configuration that meets those gates and the team's strategic role.

No new dimensions, mass budget, CAD, center of gravity or interference clearances were measured for this recommendation. A physical redesign needs sourced dimensions, interfaces, packaging and mentor engineering review before fabrication. The same-hardware software improvements in the preceding section can be evaluated first.

sections.title: 12 / Evidence, limits and reproducibility
sections.text:
## How to audit this report

**Results:** retained [TBA team 1257 match records](https://www.thebluealliance.com/team/1257/2026), retrieved October 16, 2026, with the 29 appearances shown above. Alliance scores are not individual contributions. “Tabernacle” is the event-code/location label used in the analysis; the Q11 broadcast calls it Seneca.

**Robot telemetry:** original supplied WPILOGs, their SHA-256 inventory, timestamp-integrated metrics and separate cross-log swerve scan. Q11 source SHA-256 is `f214b527dead1344b5282ca99dbf0c153d4258fa56072db0317db85d80a554b9`. The 410–425 s focus log is a viewing derivative; exact fault timing comes from the original. Ten-hertz player samples are for display and are not used to measure brief protection pulses.

**Source code:** [FRC1257/2026-Robot](https://github.com/FRC1257/2026-Robot), retained full revisions and patches. Logged Git bases with dirty working trees identify ancestry, not exact binaries. Commit dates and later branches do not prove deployment. The two GitHub images above are actual page captures; all AdvantageScope images are actual native replay captures. Code composition behavior is checked against [WPILib documentation](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/command-compositions.html).

**Video:** official FIRST Mid-Atlantic recordings, clock-aligned with roughly ±1 s uncertainty. Twelve qualification videos were available for identifiable supplied logs, eleven with gameplay alignment; Q31 is pre-match-only. Paused-frame observation records are AI review, not a completed continuous human scouting pass. This public report hosts brief illustrative stills with source links, not full broadcasts.

**Unresolved evidence:** exact PDH wiring, deployed native PDH decoder, repair notes, radio uptime/boot counters, independently sampled power, DS event logs, exact dirty source, counted shots and complete continuous video review. Raw PDH fault bits and suspect current channels are not promoted to confirmed physical failures. Raw radio authentication-bearing payloads and local filesystem details are excluded from this public artifact.

**Reproducibility retained locally:** original logs and video hashes, `software-evolution-evidence.json`, `swerve-history.json`, `q11-diagnosis-evidence.json`, video alignment receipts, source snapshots and screenshot hashes. The report's source panels provide the sanitized reviewed evidence. Recommendations are engineering judgments with testable acceptance criteria; no causal scoring gain is claimed.
